title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom at Gibeon
summary: Solomon, secure on his throne, leads all Israel to worship at Gibeon, where the old Tent of Meeting and Moses' bronze altar still stood. That night God invites him to ask for anything, and Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people. God grants it, adds riches and honor, and the chapter closes with a picture of Solomon's wealth in horses, chariots, silver, and gold.
story: Second Chronicles begins exactly where First Chronicles ended: David has died and Solomon reigns. The opening verse announces that the LORD was with him, and the first act of his reign is worship. The Chronicler wants readers to see that Solomon's greatness came from God and was meant to serve one purpose, the building of the temple that David planned. The gift of wisdom here equips him for that task, and from chapter 2 onward the story turns almost entirely to the building. This chapter is the doorway into the nine chapters on Solomon.
historical:
Solomon's reign is usually dated to about 970 to 930 BC. The parallel account in 1 Kings 3 includes details the Chronicler leaves out, such as Solomon's marriage alliance with Pharaoh's daughter, the note that the people and the king were still sacrificing at high places, and the famous judgment between two women over a baby. First Kings 1 and 2 also tell of the bloody consolidation of Solomon's power (the deaths of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei). The Chronicler compresses all of that into one line: Solomon “established himself securely over his kingdom” (verse 1).

Gibeon, about six miles (ten kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem, is identified with the site of el-Jib, where excavators found a large rock-cut pool and inscribed jar handles bearing the name Gibeon. According to Chronicles, the tabernacle Moses built had been set up there (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29), while the ark itself was in a tent David had pitched in Jerusalem. Worship in Israel was divided between two sites until the temple brought ark and altar together. The trade in horses in verses 16 and 17 involves Kue, generally identified with Cilicia in southeastern Anatolia (modern Turkey), and the Hittite and Aramean kings, the small states of northern Syria in the tenth century BC.
cultural:
A high place was an outdoor shrine, often on a hill, used for sacrifice. Later in Israel's history high places became associated with idolatry and unauthorized worship, and reforming kings tore them down. The Chronicler explains why Solomon's worship at Gibeon was legitimate: this was not any high place but the site of the Tent of Meeting and the bronze altar made by Bezalel, the craftsman who built the tabernacle furnishings in Exodus 31 and 38.

Ancient kings often sought divine guidance at the start of a reign, sometimes through a dream received at a sanctuary. A thousand burnt offerings was a royal gesture of extraordinary devotion. Horses and chariots were the most expensive military technology of the age, and a king who could buy and resell them held real power; verse 17 suggests Solomon's merchants acted as middlemen in an international trade. Silver “as common in Jerusalem as stones” (verse 15) is deliberate hyperbole, the language of royal splendor.
literary: The chapter frames a dialogue with two scenes of royal greatness. Verses 1 to 6 describe the assembly and the sacrifice, verses 7 to 12 give the night conversation between God and Solomon, and verses 13 to 17 show the promise already coming true. The dialogue turns on the verb "ask": God says “Ask, and I will give it to you!” (verse 7), Solomon asks for wisdom, and God lists what he did not ask for (riches, wealth, honor, the death of enemies, long life) before granting both what he asked and much of what he didn't. The closing verses on horses and gold appear near the end of Solomon's story in 1 Kings 10; the Chronicler places them here, right after God's promise of riches, so the reader sees the promise fulfilled at once. A near copy of the same passage returns in 2 Chronicles 9:25-28, framing Solomon's reign.

outline.t: Solomon and all Israel worship at Gibeon
God's offer and Solomon's request for wisdom
God grants wisdom and adds riches and honor

doctrines.note: Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge “so that I may lead this people” (verse 10). Wisdom in the Bible is practical skill in living and ruling under God, and here it is requested for the sake of others, not for private gain.
Solomon grounds his request in God's loving devotion to David and asks that God's promise to David be fulfilled (verses 8-9). He rules as heir to a covenant, not as a self-made king.

God's invitation to ask, and his pleasure in Solomon's request, show that God weighs not only what we ask but why. Solomon's prayer puts the good of the people and the task God gave him ahead of himself.

words.note: Chokhmah, wisdom. The word covers skill in crafts, shrewd judgment, and moral insight: the ability to see how things work and act rightly. It is the governing word of the book of Proverbs, much of which is linked with Solomon. Here it is paired with "knowledge" as the equipment of a ruler.

Madda, knowledge or understanding. It is a rare word, found mostly in late books such as Daniel and Ecclesiastes and here. Joined with wisdom, it suggests discernment, the capacity to understand situations and people well enough to govern them.

Chesed, rendered “loving devotion” in verse 8. It is the steadfast, committed love that keeps covenant faithfully, often translated lovingkindness, mercy, or steadfast love. Solomon begins by naming God's chesed to David; his whole reign rests on it.

Darash, to seek or inquire. Verse 5 says Solomon and the assembly “inquired of Him” at Gibeon. The first thing the Chronicler records of Solomon's reign is that he sought God, which in this book is the mark of a faithful king.

christ: Solomon's wisdom is a gift of God to a son of David for the sake of God's people. Isaiah later promised a shoot from Jesse's stump on whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding would rest (Isaiah 11:1-2), and the New Testament sees that promise fulfilled in Jesus. Jesus pointed to Solomon when he said that the queen of the South came to hear Solomon's wisdom and that something greater than Solomon was now present (Matthew 12:42). Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30). The invitation to ask echoes too: Jesus told his disciples to ask and it would be given, and James urges anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously (James 1:5). Solomon's gift was real but it did not keep him faithful to the end; the New Testament presents Christ as the wise king whose wisdom never failed.

hard.q: Didn't Solomon's horses from Egypt and his piles of silver and gold break the law for Israel's kings?
hard.a:
Deuteronomy 17:16-17 warns that a king must not multiply horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to get them, and must not greatly increase silver and gold. Verses 14 to 17 describe Solomon doing exactly these things. Readers take this in different ways. Some see the Chronicler, like the writer of Kings, quietly signaling the seeds of Solomon's later troubles even while celebrating his wealth; an attentive Israelite reader would have heard the echo of Deuteronomy. Others note that the Chronicler places these verses immediately after God promises Solomon riches, and read them simply as the fulfillment of that promise, with the Chronicler choosing not to dwell on Solomon's failures, which his readers already knew from 1 Kings 11. Some scholars also suggest that "Egypt" in verses 16-17 may refer to a region near Kue in Anatolia with a similar name, though this remains a minority proposal.

What is clear is that the Chronicler's portrait of Solomon is idealized for a purpose: to show the temple builder as a king blessed by God. He does not deny Solomon's faults; he simply leaves them for the book of Kings to tell.

questions: If God offered you anything, what would you ask for, and what would your request reveal about what you think you most need?
Solomon asked for wisdom so that he could serve others well. What responsibility do you carry that you need wisdom for?
God gave Solomon more than he asked. How do you hold gifts like wealth or honor when they come as a byproduct rather than a goal?
